tagline: A rough climb to a station that watched the sun.
intro: Off Eagle Eye Road, the byway turns north for the summit of Harquahala Peak, ten and a half rugged miles up the highest mountains in southwestern Arizona. It is a high-clearance, four-wheel-drive road. The top had work to do before the scientists came. The Army ran a heliograph station there in the 1880s.

The Smithsonian arrived in 1920 for the cloudless days and the distance from pollution. Its observers measured the sun's energy for five years, then moved to Table Mountain in California for easier access and better air.
season: BLM recommends November through April; summer temperatures can reach 115 degrees.

moments.title: Old mining ground
moments.text: On the way up, the drive passes the leavings of earlier miners: old debris, shafts and stone houses.

moments.title: Harquahala Peak Observatory
moments.text: At the summit, corrugated tin covers the two-story adobe observatory, where scientists measured the sun's energy above plains lying thousands of feet below.

moments.title: Summit pack trail
moments.text: From the summit a pack trail leads down the mountain into the Harquahala Wilderness, with several steep and difficult stretches.

practical: High-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles are required, and there is no drinking water.
